questions.question: Which radiographic feature is a hallmark of conventional osteoarthritis and helps distinguish it from inflammatory arthritis?
questions.detail: Osteoarthritis is characterized by subchondral sclerosis due to reactive bone remodeling. It classically features a lack of periarticular osteopenia, which is a hallmark of inflammatory conditions like RA.

questions.question: In the hand, which joint is most commonly affected by conventional osteoarthritis?
questions.detail: The order of involvement in hand OA is DIP joints > 1st CMC joint > PIP joints. Unlike RA, the MCP joints are typically spared in osteoarthritis.

questions.question: What is the characteristic radiographic appearance of erosive osteoarthritis in the DIP joints?
questions.detail: Central erosions combined with marginal osteophytes at the DIP joints create the classic 'gull-wing' appearance in erosive osteoarthritis.

questions.question: What is the most common pattern of femoral head migration in hip osteoarthritis?
questions.detail: Hip OA most commonly causes superior-lateral cartilage space narrowing, leading to superolateral migration of the femoral head. Axial migration is more typical of Rheumatoid Arthritis.

questions.question: In rheumatoid arthritis, where do marginal erosions first occur?
questions.detail: RA erosions first occur at the 'bare area,' which is a region of exposed bone within the joint capsule not covered by thick cartilage.

questions.question: Which radiographic finding is the earliest change associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis?
questions.detail: The earliest radiographic changes of RA are soft-tissue swelling and periarticular osteopenia, reflecting underlying synovitis and hyperemia.

questions.question: A patient with advanced RA presents with flexion at the PIP joint and hyperextension at the DIP joint. This is known as:
questions.detail: Boutonnière deformity is defined by PIP flexion and DIP hyperextension. Swan neck deformity is the opposite: PIP hyperextension and DIP flexion.

questions.question: What defines a 'protrusio deformity' in a female patient with severe hip RA?
choices: Medial deviation of the femoral head >1 mm beyond the ilioischial line
Medial deviation of the femoral head >3 mm beyond the ilioischial line
Medial deviation of the femoral head >6 mm beyond the ilioischial line
Axial migration with preserved joint space
Lateral subluxation of the femoral head
questions.detail: Protrusio deformity is defined as medial deviation >3 mm in males and >6 mm in females beyond the ilioischial line.

questions.question: What is the most common direction of atlantoaxial subluxation in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
questions.detail: Anterior subluxation is the most common direction and is caused by inflammation and resultant laxity of the transverse ligament.

questions.question: Which finding in the spine is considered pathognomonic for degenerative disc change?
questions.detail: The presence of gas in the intervertebral disc (vacuum phenomenon) is a classic sign of degenerative change.

questions.question: Unlike Rheumatoid Arthritis, Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) has a higher propensity for which finding in the wrist?
questions.detail: While late-stage RA may uncommonly cause ankylosis, JIA has a higher propensity for carpal ankylosis.

questions.question: In RA of the knee, which compartment is typically affected?
questions.detail: RA causes symmetrical cartilage space narrowing involving all three joint spaces in the knee. OA tends to first affect the medial compartment.

questions.question: Posterior atlantoaxial subluxation in a patient with RA is most likely due to:
questions.detail: While anterior subluxation is due to ligament laxity, posterior subluxation in RA is usually due to odontoid erosion.

questions.question: The 'outside-in' theory of RA pathogenesis suggests erosions begin where?
choices: Just inside the synovium at the bare area
questions.detail: Synovial joint anatomy shows the bare area just inside the synovium is the site of first erosions in RA.

questions.question: Which hand joint is classically spared in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
questions.detail: RA commonly involves the MCPs, PIPs, and carpals, but the DIPs are usually spared.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is associated with symmetric sacroiliitis?
questions.detail: Symmetric sacroiliitis is caused by Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) and IBD-associated arthropathy (both start with vowels).

questions.question: Asymmetric sacroiliitis is a hallmark of which condition?
questions.detail: Asymmetric sacroiliitis is characteristic of Psoriatic Arthritis and Reactive Arthritis (both start with consonants).

questions.question: A 'Romanus lesion' in ankylosing spondylitis refers to:
choices: Sclerosis of the entire vertebral body
Erosion of the anterior superior margin of a vertebral body
Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament
questions.detail: A Romanus lesion is an erosion at the discovertebral junction; the subsequent sclerosis at this site is the 'shiny corner sign'.

questions.question: What is the classic radiographic sign of late-stage ankylosing spondylitis involving the spine?
questions.detail: The 'bamboo spine' appearance in AS is caused by thin, vertical, symmetric bridging syndesmophytes.

questions.question: In psoriatic arthritis, the radiographic hallmark in the hand is:
questions.detail: Pencil-in-cup erosions, most common at the DIP joints, are a hallmark of psoriatic arthritis.

questions.question: A 'sausage digit' is a characteristic radiographic finding for:
questions.detail: Diffuse soft-tissue swelling of an entire digit produces the characteristic sausage digit in psoriatic arthritis.

questions.question: Reactive arthropathy (formerly Reiter disease) predominantly affects which area?
questions.detail: Reactive arthropathy predominantly affects the feet, often involving the calcaneus with fluffy periosteal reaction and enthesophytes.

questions.question: What is the key radiographic finding of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) in the hands?
choices: Reducible subluxations in the absence of erosive change
questions.detail: SLE is characterized by reducible subluxations (often swan neck deformities) without erosions, distinguishing it from RA.

questions.question: Which condition is characterized by intramuscular and subcutaneous soft-tissue calcifications?
questions.detail: The imaging hallmark of Polymyositis and Dermatomyositis is extensive soft-tissue calcification, particularly intramuscular.

questions.question: Acro-osteolysis (distal tuft resorption) combined with soft tissue calcification is characteristic of:
questions.detail: Scleroderma typically presents with acro-osteolysis and soft tissue calcification.

questions.question: The 'main-en-lorgnette' or opera-glass hand deformity is a severe manifestation of:
questions.detail: This severe variant causes marked deformity and telescoping digits, also known as opera-glass hand.

questions.question: Symmetrical erosions and widening of the SI joints in a young man with back stiffness is the earliest sign of:
questions.detail: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) predominantly affects young men and presents with early symmetric SI joint changes.

questions.question: Which inflammatory arthritis is thought to be a sequela of infectious diarrhea or urethritis?
questions.detail: Reactive arthropathy is thought to follow specific gastrointestinal or genitourinary infections.

questions.question: The 'dagger sign' in the spine is associated with which condition?
questions.detail: The dagger sign is associated with Ankylosing Spondylitis due to ossification of the interspinous ligaments.

questions.question: Unilateral sacroiliitis should raise immediate suspicion for:
questions.detail: An important cause of unilateral sacroiliitis is septic arthritis, particularly in immunocompromised patients or IV drug users.

questions.question: Which radiographic finding is the hallmark of Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition (CPPD) disease?
questions.detail: Chondrocalcinosis (calcification of hyaline or fibrocartilage) is the hallmark of CPPD.

questions.question: In CPPD of the hand, where are hook-like osteophytes typically located?
choices: Radial aspect of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpal heads
Distal aspect of the PIP joints
Volar aspect of the DIP joints
questions.detail: CPPD characteristically produces hook-like osteophytes from the radial aspect of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpal heads.

questions.question: Advanced CPPD arthritis in the wrist can lead to which pattern of carpal instability?
questions.detail: Advanced CPP arthritis features fragmentation of the scaphoid and proximal migration of the capitate, resulting in SLAC arthropathy.

questions.question: Gouty erosions are classically described as:
questions.detail: Gout produces juxta-articular erosions with overhanging edges (tophi) while often preserving joint space until late stages.

questions.question: What is the 'double contour sign' on ultrasound indicative of?
questions.detail: The double contour sign represents urate crystals deposited on the hyperechoic cartilage surface.

questions.question: Milwaukee shoulder is a destructive arthritis characterized by the deposition of which crystal?
questions.detail: Milwaukee shoulder is a rare intra-articular variant of calcium hydroxyapatite deposition leading to rapid shoulder destruction.

questions.question: Which arthropathy features joint space widening in its early stages due to cartilage hypertrophy?
questions.detail: In contrast to all other arthropathies, acromegaly causes early joint space widening.

questions.question: The 'shoulder-pad sign' is a clinical finding associated with:
questions.detail: Bulky soft-tissue nodules in the shoulder superimposed on atrophic muscles produce the shoulder-pad sign.

questions.question: What is a characteristic radiographic finding of hemophilic arthropathy in the elbow?
choices: Enlarged radial head and widened trochlear notch
Subchondral cysts of the coronoid process
questions.detail: Chronic articular hyperemia in hemophilia leads to characteristic overgrowth changes like an enlarged radial head and widened trochlear notch.

questions.question: Which joint is most commonly affected by the hypertrophic variant of neuropathic arthropathy in diabetic patients?
questions.detail: Diabetes-related neuropathic arthropathy (Charcot joint) typically affects the foot and ankle.

questions.question: The atrophic variant of neuropathic arthropathy, featuring humeral head resorption, is classically associated with:
questions.detail: The atrophic variant of neuropathic arthropathy in the shoulder is classic for syringomyelia.

questions.question: Primary synovial osteochondromatosis is characterized by intra-articular bodies that are:
choices: Located only in the small joints of the hand
questions.detail: The hallmark of primary synovial osteochondromatosis is multiple bodies of similar size and shape, whereas those in OA are fewer and varied.

questions.question: Which finding distinguishes diabetic foot osteomyelitis from Charcot arthropathy?
choices: Bony cortex disruption and presence of a sinus tract
questions.detail: Osteomyelitis is almost always associated with a cutaneous ulcer and sinus tract, whereas Charcot joints usually have an intact cortex.

questions.question: In a patient with an acute mono-articular arthritis, which fluid WBC count is 92% specific for septic arthritis?
questions.detail: A fluid WBC count of >50,000 is highly specific (92%) for septic arthritis.

questions.question: 'Spadelike' enlargement of the terminal tufts of the distal phalanges is characteristic of:
questions.detail: Excess growth hormone in acromegaly leads to characteristic spadelike enlargement of the distal tufts.
